edits.text: - Fallback ordering: when one marker falls immediately before or inside a numeral/quantity, unit/measurement, date/time, or location/directional phrase that completes the preceding noun or verb phrase, prefer any other marker in the sentence over that marker; if no other marker is available, prefer a cut after the completing phrase rather than before it.

- Fallback ordering: when comparing two candidate cuts where one lies between a clause's subject or auxiliary and its main verb, or between a predicate and an immediately following essential complement, negation (e.g. "not") or exception marker (e.g. "except", "but"), prefer the cut that falls after the verb plus its immediately following complement/negation/exception token over the cut that falls before it.

- Keep the preceding noun or verb head together with any immediately following numeral/quantity, measurement unit, date/time, or location/directional phrase that completes or specifies it (i.e. when a cut falls immediately before or inside such a completing expression).

- Keep a clause's subject (an NP or pronoun immediately before a verb) together with the immediately following auxiliary or main verb that completes its truth‑conditional core. Keep a verb or predicate together with any immediately following essential complements or scope markers (e.g. 'not', 'except', 'but').

- Keep a preceding head (a noun phrase head or a verb token) together with any immediately following numeral/quantity, unit/measurement, date/time, or locative/directional phrase that completes or specifies that head.

- Prefer a cut that falls after an immediately following numeral, quantity/unit/measurement, date/time, parenthesized measurement, or locative/directional phrase which completes the preceding noun or verb phrase, over a cut that falls immediately before or inside that completing phrase.

edits._was: - Does the stretch after the cut supply disambiguating information (names, numbers, polarity markers, complements) essential to interpret an earlier ambiguous NP or verb phrase?
